summary.text: If $2^N+1$ is prime, its totient is $2^N$ and the general bound $\varphi(m)<m$ makes it minimal. Otherwise, any smaller candidate than $2^{N+1}$ would be odd with totient exactly $2^N$; it must be squarefree, and each prime factor has the form $2^{2^c}+1$, so $N=2^{33}$ would be a sum of at least two distinct powers of two, which after factoring out the least one gives an odd divisor greater than $1$ of a power of two—a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler's totient function, and for \(n\ge 0\) define
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We prove a slightly more general statement. Let \(K\ge 1\), put
\[
N=2^K,\qquad X=2^N,
\]
and let
\[
F=2^N+1=X+1.
\]
We will prove
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
X+1,&\text{if }X+1\text{ is prime},\\
2X=2^{N+1},&\text{if }X+1\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Taking \(K=33\) gives the desired result because then \(N=2^{33}\) and
\[
F=2^{2^{33}}+1=F_{33}.
\]

We use the following elementary facts about Euler's totient.

1. If \(r>0\), then \(\varphi(r)>0\); if \(r>1\), then \(\varphi(r)<r\).

2. If \(p\) is prime, then
\[
\varphi(p)=p-1,
\qquad
\varphi(p^e)=p^{e-1}(p-1)\quad(e\ge1).
\]
In particular, a positive integer \(r\) is prime exactly when \(\varphi(r)=r-1\).

3. The totient is multiplicative on coprime factors. Thus, if \(r\) is squarefree with distinct prime factors \(p_1,\dots,p_t\), then
\[
\varphi(r)=\prod_{i=1}^t(p_i-1).
\]

4. If \(d\mid r\), then \(\varphi(d)\mid\varphi(r)\). This can be seen directly from prime factorizations: for every prime \(p\), if \(p^a\mid d\) and \(p^b\mid r\) are the exact corresponding prime powers, then \(a\le b\), and
\(p^{a-1}(p-1)\) divides \(p^{b-1}(p-1)\); multiplying over the prime factors of \(d\) proves the assertion.

We first establish some bounds that will identify the only possible numbers below \(2X\).

For every \(k\ge0\),
\[
\varphi(2k)\le k. \tag{1}
\]
One proof is by strong induction on \(k\). The assertion is immediate for \(k=0\). If \(k\) is odd, then \(2\) and \(k\) are coprime, so
\[
\varphi(2k)=\varphi(2)\varphi(k)=\varphi(k)\le k.
\]
If \(k\) is even, write \(k=2j\). For \(k>0\), we have \(j<k\), and the prime-power formula at the prime \(2\), together with multiplicativity for the odd part, gives
\[
\varphi(4j)=2\varphi(2j).
\]
By induction \(\varphi(2j)\le j\), so \(\varphi(4j)\le2j=k\). This proves (1).

Now suppose that \(m>0\), that
\[
X=2^N\mid\varphi(m), \tag{2}
\]
and that
\[
m<2X=2^{N+1}. \tag{3}
\]
Then \(m\) must be odd. Indeed, if \(m=2k\), condition (3) gives \(k<X\), while (1) gives
\[
0<\varphi(m)=\varphi(2k)\le k<X.
\]
This is incompatible with the positive integer \(\varphi(m)\) being divisible by \(X\).

Under the same hypotheses, we also have
\[
\varphi(m)=X. \tag{4}
\]
Since \(N\ge1\), \(X\ge2\). The number \(m\) cannot be \(1\), because \(X\nmid\varphi(1)=1\). Hence \(m>1\), and therefore
\[
\varphi(m)<m<2X.
\]
On the other hand, (2) and positivity imply \(\varphi(m)\ge X\). The only positive multiple of \(X\) that is strictly less than \(2X\) is \(X\) itself, proving (4).

We will also need the universal lower bound
\[
m\ge X+1 \tag{5}
\]
for every positive \(m\) satisfying (2), whether or not \(m<2X\). Again \(m\ne1\), and hence
\[
X\le\varphi(m)<m,
\]
which, since the quantities are integers, yields (5).

There is one more elementary structural fact about primes of the form \(2^v+1\): if \(v>0\) and \(2^v+1\) is prime, then \(v\) is a power of two. To prove this, write
\[
v=2^c q
\]
where \(q\) is odd. If \(q>1\), let \(A=2^{2^c}>1\). Since \(q\) is odd,
\[
A+1\mid A^q+1=2^v+1,
\]
because
\[
A^q+1=(A+1)(A^{q-1}-A^{q-2}+\cdots-A+1).
\]
Both factors are then nontrivial, contradicting primality. Thus \(q=1\) and \(v=2^c\).

We now determine the minimum.

First suppose that \(F=X+1\) is prime. Then
\[
\varphi(F)=F-1=X,
\]
so \(F\) is an admissible value in the definition of \(a(N)\). Conversely, every admissible \(m\) satisfies (5), namely \(m\ge X+1=F\). Therefore
\[
a(N)=F=X+1
\]
in the prime case.

Now suppose that \(F=X+1\) is not prime. The number \(2X=2^{N+1}\) is admissible, since the prime-power formula gives
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N=X.
\]
Thus \(a(N)\le2X\). It remains to prove that no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(2X\).

Assume for contradiction that some \(m>0\) satisfies
\[
X\mid\varphi(m),\qquad m<2X. \tag{6}
\]
The preceding reductions show that
\[
m\text{ is odd},\qquad \varphi(m)=X,
\qquad m\ge X+1. \tag{7}
\]
If \(m=X+1=F\), then \(\varphi(F)=X=F-1\), which would imply that \(F\) is prime, contrary to the current hypothesis. Hence
\[
m>X+1. \tag{8}
\]
The number \(m\) cannot itself be prime: if it were, then
\[
X=\varphi(m)=m-1,
\]
so \(m=X+1\), contradicting (8). Thus \(m\) is composite.

We next show that \(m\) is squarefree. Suppose that a prime \(p\) satisfies \(p^2\mid m\). By divisibility of totients,
\[
\varphi(p^2)=p(p-1)\mid\varphi(m)=X=2^N.
\]
Consequently \(p\mid2^N\), so the prime \(p\) must be \(2\). But \(m\) is odd, so \(2\nmid m\), a contradiction. No square of a prime divides \(m\), and hence \(m\) is squarefree.

Let its distinct prime factors be
\[
p_1,p_2,\dots,p_t.
\]
Because \(m\) is composite and squarefree, \(t\ge2\). Every \(p_i\) is odd, since \(m\) is odd. Moreover, from \(p_i\mid m\) and divisibility of totients we obtain
\[
p_i-1=\varphi(p_i)\mid\varphi(m)=2^N.
\]
Every divisor of a power of two is itself a power of two, so for some integer \(v_i\ge0\),
\[
p_i-1=2^{v_i},
\qquad	ext{or equivalently}\qquad
p_i=2^{v_i}+1. \tag{9}
\]
Since \(p_i\) is odd, it is not \(2\), and therefore \(v_i>0\). The structural fact just proved now applies to the prime \(p_i=2^{v_i}+1\): there is some \(c_i\ge0\) such that
\[
v_i=2^{c_i}.
\]
Thus every prime factor of \(m\) is a Fermat-type prime
\[
p_i=2^{2^{c_i}}+1. \tag{10}
\]
The integers \(c_1,\dots,c_t\) are pairwise distinct. Indeed, equality \(c_i=c_j\) would make the right-hand sides of (10) equal, hence \(p_i=p_j\), contrary to the fact that these are distinct prime factors.

Since \(m\) is squarefree, multiplicativity of the totient and (10) give
\[
\varphi(m)
 =\prod_{i=1}^t(p_i-1)
 =\prod_{i=1}^t 2^{2^{c_i}}
 =2^{\sum_{i=1}^t2^{c_i}}.
\]
But \(\varphi(m)=X=2^N\). Exponentiation by \(2\) is injective on nonnegative integer exponents, so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^t2^{c_i}=N=2^K. \tag{11}
\]
Thus a single power of two has been represented as a sum of at least two distinct powers of two. We finish by showing directly that this is impossible.

Let \(c_0\) be the least of the distinct integers \(c_1,\dots,c_t\). Separate the corresponding summand \(2^{c_0}\) in (11). Every other \(c_i\) is at least \(c_0+1\), so every other summand is divisible by \(2^{c_0+1}\). Since there is at least one other summand, their sum is
\[
2^{c_0+1}M
\]
for some positive integer \(M\). Equation (11) becomes
\[
2^{c_0}+2^{c_0+1}M=2^K,
\]
or
\[
2^{c_0}(1+2M)=2^K. \tag{12}
\]
Therefore the odd integer \(1+2M\) divides \(2^K\). But every divisor of \(2^K\) is a power of two, and the only odd power of two is \(1\). This is impossible because \(M>0\), so \(1+2M>1\). The contradiction proves that no admissible \(m<2X\) exists.

Since \(2X\) itself is admissible, it follows that in the nonprime case
\[
a(N)=2X=2^{N+1}.
\]

Finally take \(K=33\). Then
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad X=2^N=2^{2^{33}},
\qquad F=X+1=2^{2^{33}}+1=F_{33}.
\]
The general result therefore says
\[
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
which is exactly the conjectured formula.
